\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals \textit{improve} over in-domain levels: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain 0.386, $\Delta{=}{+}0.083$) and the structural average rises from $\rho{=}0.335$ to $0.377$.
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (greedy F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer.}
The reverse direction collapses: CoNLL$\to$SciERC yields greedy F1${=}0.009$, and most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations.
Only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$); all others are negative.
This confirms a schema incompatibility boundary: a model trained on a narrow schema cannot produce meaningful structured outputs for a wider schema, and confidence signals---which measure inter-sample agreement---become misleading when the model systematically generates incorrect but consistent outputs.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The asymmetry is directional, not symmetric: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the model's broader coverage subsumes the target, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the model lacks the entity types needed for the target schema.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite for meaningful quality estimation.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals across quality estimation, binary discrimination, and sample selection for LLM-based structured IE, revealing that these metrics decouple---single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves sample selection despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
The instance-level failure of four signals is definitional; the empirical finding is that neither consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) nor log-probability bridges the gap.
MBR utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them; LP scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
A controlled free-form decoding ablation confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
Signal rankings shift with task difficulty---EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude; at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse to non-significance.
RE findings rest on SciERC alone (preliminary) and warrant multi-benchmark validation.
Trained verifiers, scaling to 70B+ models, and conformal prediction are promising directions for closing the gap.

## 论文全文

### Title
Strong Predictors, Weak Selectors: Why Confidence Signals Do Not Scale Structured Information Extraction

### Abstract
Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
We compare five confidence signals across NER and relation extraction on three benchmarks with two 8B-parameter model families and uncover a \textit{correlation-selection gap}: signals achieve strong quality estimation yet none significantly improves sample selection despite substantial oracle headroom.
Most signals are instance-level by construction and cannot rank candidates; the empirical question is whether log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---or consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) can bridge the gap.
Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties, while MBR utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
A controlled ablation confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
Signal rankings depend on task complexity, with findings consistent across two model families at 8B scale.

### Introduction (contributions)
C1: A systematic evaluation framework — five signals × three metrics, showing decoupling
C2: The correlation-selection gap and its diagnosis — MBR + LP compression as core empirical contributions, instance-level failure is definitional
C3: Task-complexity boundary conditions — EM/SJ crossover, WNUT-17 collapse, extending Nédellec et al.

### Method
Five signals: LP (per-sample, model-internal), EM/FK (surface, instance-level), SJ/VC (structural, instance-level). FK independence: "mild negative dependence" (not positive correlation). Evaluation: ρ + AUROC for QE, best-of-N F1 for selection.

### Experiments
- Quality estimation: VC ρ=0.379 (SciERC NER), EM AUROC=0.749; difficulty-dependent crossover (EM>SJ on CoNLL, SJ>EM on SciERC)
- Selection gap: LP best at 0.650 NER F1 but p=0.39 vs greedy 0.644; oracle 0.776 (13.2pp headroom)
- WNUT-17: VC full-set ρ=0.724 but conditional ρ=0.038 (n.s.); LP negative ρ=-0.410
- Robustness: structural > LP across all NER settings; RE only VC > LP (preliminary)

### Discussion
- Two-layer gap: Layer 1 definitional (4/5 instance-level), Layer 2 score compression (intrinsic)
- MBR connection: utility-quality misalignment at per-sample level
- Ablation: free-form LP variance ratio 0.97×, NER selection +0.18pp (negligible); RE LP flips +1.69pp (single seed caveat)
- OOD: structural signals robust under wider→narrower schema transfer (VC ρ=0.469 OOD vs 0.386 in-domain); reverse fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure
- N=16: SJ converges with VC (Δ=0.002), lower σ (0.010 vs 0.026)

### Conclusion
Mirrors C1-C3 structure: framework → gap+diagnosis (MBR+LP) → task-complexity. "Do Not" framing. Future: verifiers, 70B+, conformal prediction.

### Limitations
RE single benchmark, 8B only, unsupervised signals only, N≤16, SJ-FK gap 0.003 on CoNLL LLaMA, ablation single dataset, thinking token confound, LP temperature sensitivity uncharacterized.

### Appendix (new sections)
- §app:n_scaling: 3 tables — N=8 vs N=16 ρ comparison (Qwen3-8B SciERC), Kendall's W ranking stability (W=1.000 at N=8, 0.956 at N=16), cross-seed σ comparison (-32% NER, -24% RE)
- §app:ood: Cross-dataset OOD analysis — SciERC→CoNLL (all signals significant p<0.001, VC ρ=0.469), CoNLL→SciERC excluded (catastrophic model failure, greedy F1=0.009). In-domain baselines sourced from Table 1 (same model/seed/N).

\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).

The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific rather than universal.
Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
